title: The bitter cucumber
hook: a cucumber is bitter? put it down; briars in the path? step aside (Meditations 8.50)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said it's not the thing that disturbs you, but your judgment of it. Your line was not the thing, my view. Which complaint did you rephrase? Day two hundred nine.

You bite into a sandwich and the lettuce is gone slimy. You could put it down. Or you could hold it up and say to the room: why? Why does this always happen? Who packs a sandwich like this? What's wrong with this whole store? Five minutes later, you're still holding the sandwich. Some of us are very gifted at turning small annoyances into long speeches. Marcus, it seems, knew the habit. So he gave himself a short, dry bit of advice. It starts with a vegetable. Today: cucumber.
screen: `THE SLIMY LETTUCE.` → `A LONG SPEECH ABOUT A SANDWICH.` → `THE BITTER CUCUMBER.`

segments.voice: Book Eight, section fifty, in George Long's translation: "A cucumber is bitter. Throw it away. There are briers in the road. Turn aside from them." Then Marcus says: this is enough. Don't add, and why were such things ever made? That's the whole trick. The first part is action. Bitter? Put it down. Thorny path? Go around. The second part is what not to add: the speech. The why me. The why is the world like this. Marcus even has a joke about it. If you asked why there are bitter cucumbers, he says, someone who understands nature would laugh at you. It would be like walking into a carpenter's shop and complaining about the wood shavings on the floor, or into a shoemaker's and complaining about the leather scraps. Of course there are scraps. That's what a workshop looks like when things are being made. For the Stoics, the world is nature's workshop, and bitter cucumbers and briars are some of the shavings. This connects to yesterday. Yesterday was about the judgment you add to a thing. Today is simpler. Some things don't even need a new judgment. They need a small movement: put it down, step aside, carry on. You don't have to understand why the cucumber is bitter. You don't have to fix the briars. You don't have to make it mean something about your life. There's a lightness to it, almost funny. A lot of annoyances are cucumbers. Your line: step aside.
screen: `BITTER? THROW IT AWAY.` · `DON'T ADD: WHY WAS THIS MADE?` · `SHAVINGS ON THE WORKSHOP FLOOR.` · then, large: `STEP ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step around one annoyance. Settle, and let a small, familiar annoyance come to mind. The noisy neighbor, the slow app, the sock that's always inside out. Notice the speech that usually comes with it. Then picture yourself simply putting it down, or stepping around it, with no speech at all. Feel how light that is. Breathe there. The bell holds the time.
Cucumber. Marcus says if a cucumber is bitter, throw it away; if there are briars in the road, turn aside, and don't ask why. Today's word.
Your line: step aside. Today, when a small annoyance shows up, handle it in one move, and skip the speech. Day two hundred nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this line for small daily irritations: deal with the thing simply, and skip the added complaint about why the world contains it.
